### Priya's Impossible Deadline

Priya stared at her laptop screen and felt the familiar tightness in her chest. Her advisor had just sent a deceptively cheerful email: "Let's target a submission to the NeurIPS workshop. You'll need a full literature review on retrieval-augmented generation, reproduce three key baselines, and write up a coherent synthesis. Deadline: two weeks." Two weeks. For work that would normally take two months.

She knew how to do each piece individually. She could prompt ChatGPT to summarize a paper. She could write Python to load a dataset and fine-tune a model. She could search Google Scholar for citations. But the real problem was not any single step. It was the *orchestration*. She found herself copying and pasting between twelve browser tabs, a Jupyter notebook, a shared Google Doc, and a Slack thread with her labmate. She would ask the LLM to summarize a paper, then realize she needed to check whether the paper's claims matched a table in a different paper. That meant searching for the second paper. That meant refining her search query. That meant remembering what she had already searched for. Every ten minutes, she lost her train of thought.

After two days of this, Priya had a revelation that felt obvious in hindsight. She did not need a better LLM. She needed an LLM that could *do* things: (a) search databases; (b) read PDFs; (c) write and run code; (d) remember what it had already done; and (e) figure out what to do next. Not a chatbot that waited passively for her next question, but something more like a research assistant with a mind of its own. What if she could describe her goal ("find the top 20 papers on RAG published since 2023, reproduce the three most-cited baselines, and write a synthesis") and have an AI system break that goal into subtasks, execute them in the right order, recover from mistakes, and produce a polished result?

This is not science fiction. Systems that do exactly this exist today: coding agents that fix real GitHub issues, computer-use agents that operate desktop applications, and multi-agent teams that collaborate on complex research tasks. But here is the puzzle that will occupy us for this entire chapter. The gap between "an LLM that answers questions well" and "an LLM that reliably completes a 50-step autonomous workflow" turns out to be staggeringly large. The best computer-use agents in 2025 succeed at roughly 12% of the tasks that humans complete 72% of the time. Coding agents that score 53% on curated benchmarks crumble on real-world codebases. Agents that pass 70% of trials individually drop below 25% when you require them to succeed consistently across eight independent runs. What explains this gap, and what would it take to close it?

![Different uses of large language models. **A**: In NLP, an LLM takes text as input and outputs text. **B**: Language agents place the LLM in a feedback loop with the external environment. **C**: Cognitive language agents additionally use the LLM to manage internal state via learning and reasoning. This chapter unpacks each of these transitions. Source: Sumers et al. (2023), Figure 1.](LLM and VLM Agentic Systems/images/coala-lang-agent-progression.png){#fig-lang-agent-progression}



### Chapter Overview

The word "agent" has become one of the most overloaded terms in AI. In 2023, it meant a chatbot with a web search plugin. In 2024, it meant a multi-step coding assistant. By early 2026, it seems to mean anything that calls an API more than once. This chapter cuts through the hype to map the actual intellectual terrain of LLM-based agentic systems, from the foundational papers that defined the field to the research frontiers that remain genuinely open.

Here is a pattern that recurs throughout: many of the systems that receive the most attention (Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT with tools, Google's Mariner) are *engineering compositions* of the foundational ideas from 2022-2023, not fundamentally new research contributions. This is not a criticism; good engineering is essential. But the genuinely seminal contributions are those that introduce (a) new *abstractions*; (b) new *capabilities*; (c) new *evaluation paradigms*; or (d) new *meta-approaches*. One of this chapter's goals is to help you tell those apart.

The chapter follows Priya's journey as her research assistant grows in capability. We start by (a) formalizing what makes something an "agent" (@sec-what-is-an-agent); (b) building up the reasoning backbone (@sec-reasoning-and-acting), tools and memory (@sec-tools-memory-grounding), and multi-agent coordination (@sec-multi-agent); (c) benchmarking against real-world tasks and confronting the reliability gap (@sec-real-world-agents); (d) mapping every concept to agent products you already use daily (@sec-agents-in-practice); and (e) closing with the research frontiers that could transform the field (@sec-frontiers).

**Prerequisites:** You should (a) be comfortable with the Transformer architecture at a high level; (b) know what Chain-of-Thought prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) are; and (c) have a basic RL vocabulary (policy, reward, value function). We define all notation as we go.

### Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

- Distinguish between an LLM, a tool-augmented LLM, and a true LLM agent using the CoALA framework's three dimensions: memory, action space, and decision procedure
- Explain the reasoning spectrum from Chain-of-Thought through ReAct to Tree of Thoughts and Reflexion, and identify which approach fits which type of task
- Describe how agents acquire and use tools (Toolformer's self-supervised approach, function calling, the MCP protocol) and why the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) matters as much as model capability
- Analyze the memory hierarchy in LLM agents (working, episodic, semantic, procedural) and explain the designs of Generative Agents and MemGPT
- Evaluate when multi-agent architectures (debate, role-playing, orchestration) genuinely improve over a single agent, and when they introduce unnecessary overhead
- Interpret agent benchmark results (SWE-bench, OSWorld, AgentBench, $\tau$-bench) and explain the reliability gap between single-trial and multi-trial success rates
- Identify the three most important research frontiers: training agents with RL, automated agent design (ADAS), and agent safety

### Notation

| Symbol | Meaning | First used |
|---|---|---|
| $a_t$ | Action at time step $t$ | @sec-reasoning-and-acting |
| $o_t$ | Observation at time step $t$ | @sec-reasoning-and-acting |
| $c_t$ | Context (including thought traces) at time step $t$ | @sec-reasoning-and-acting |
| $\text{mem}_t$ | Agent memory state at trial $t$ | @sec-reasoning-and-acting |
| $V(s)$ | Value function for state/thought $s$ in tree search | @sec-reasoning-and-acting |
| $e_i = (a_c, i_c)$ | API call token and input in Toolformer | @sec-tools-memory-grounding |
| $L^+(e_i), L^-(e_i)$ | Language modeling loss with/without API result | @sec-tools-memory-grounding |
| $\tau$ | Threshold for API call insertion (Toolformer) or benchmark name ($\tau$-bench) | @sec-tools-memory-grounding, @sec-real-world-agents |
| $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ | Weights for recency, importance, relevance in Generative Agents retrieval | @sec-tools-memory-grounding |
| $L_t$ | Orchestrator ledger at step $t$ (Magentic-One) | @sec-multi-agent |
| $\pi_\theta$ | Agent policy parameterized by $\theta$ | @sec-frontiers |
| $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ | Reference policy for KL regularization | @sec-frontiers |
| $F(\text{agent})$ | Fitness function for agent architecture search (ADAS) | @sec-frontiers |
